summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create an independent statutory body to oversee how parliamentarians and their staff spend public money on work expenses.
The body, governed by a board appointed by the Governor-General, would advise on, monitor, administer, report on, audit and make rulings about travel and work expenses.
An independent review of the new authority would be conducted three years after the bill starts.
changes: Establishes the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority as an independent statutory authority.
Gives the authority functions including advising, monitoring, administering, reporting, auditing and making rulings on work expenses.
Provides for an independent review of the authority three years after commencement.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: The Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority Bill 2017 establishes an independent body to oversee and audit parliamentarians' work expenses, with monthly reporting replacing six-monthly disclosures from 1 July 2017. An interim advisory body will operate until the authority commences.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: The bill provides exemptions from freedom of information laws for the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority to allow it to give frank personal advice to parliamentarians and their staff on travel expenses and allowances, encouraging early engagement.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: The opposition supported the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority Bill 2017, which establishes an independent body to monitor and manage parliamentarians' travel and work expenses, and criticised the government for delaying implementation of the 2015 Conde review recommendations for nearly a year after scandals involving Bronwyn Bishop and the member for Farrer.

speeches.speaker: Emma Husar
speeches.brief: The member for Lindsay argued for entitlements reform to restore public trust, supporting the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority Bill 2017 and the removal of the Life Gold Pass, while citing Bronwyn Bishop’s “choppergate”, the former health minister’s Gold Coast getaways, and 36 recommendations from a review that have been before the Prime Minister for nearly a year.

speeches.speaker: Julian Hill
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority Bill 2017 will provide clear, frank advice and rulings on entitlements, unlike the current confusing system, and criticised the government for delaying action since the Bronwyn Bishop scandal in 2015.

speeches.speaker: Cathy McGowan
speeches.brief: The member supported the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority Bill 2017 and the amendments from the member for Mayo, but argued the government had not gone far enough. She called for consolidating parliamentary entitlement rules into a single principles-based Act of Parliament, citing prior reviews and research on declining public trust.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the bills to establish the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority (IPEA) will improve transparency and public trust, while noting that 87% of current MPs—those elected after 2004—no longer receive a pension or generous travel allowances. He welcomed the authority for clarifying expense rules and providing a reference point for MPs, though he cautioned that oversight costs may exceed savings.

speeches.speaker: Darren Chester
speeches.brief: The Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2017 is the first step in the biggest reforms to managing parliamentarians' expenses in more than a generation, establishing a new authority to provide clear guidance and ensure accountability. The government will continue implementing recommendations from an independent entitlements review, and a consequential amendment to the Freedom of Information Act will allow the authority to give confidential advice on travel expenses.
